_note: Meanings for the later Nyāya texts (Vācaspati, Gaṅgeśa, Annaṃbhaṭṭa and their commentators). Same format as curated.json. Entries here are used for every text except the Nyāyasūtra-Bhāṣya, where they only fill gaps, so that Gautama's own technical senses (e.g. jāti = futile rejoinder) are kept there.

jāti.n: In the Nyāyasūtra jāti means a futile rejoinder; from Vaiśeṣika onward it is the ordinary word for a universal (= sāmānya).

padārtha.n: Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika counts seven: substance, quality, motion, universal, particularity, inherence and absence.

pramā: valid cognition, true knowledge (a cognition of a thing as having the feature it really has)

vyāpti.m: pervasion, invariable concomitance (of probans with probandum)
vyāpti.n: ‘Where there is smoke there is fire’: the probans is pervaded (vyāpya), the probandum is the pervader (vyāpaka).

vyāpya: pervaded — what never occurs without the other (the probans, e.g. smoke)
vyāpaka: pervader — what is present wherever the other is (the probandum, e.g. fire)
vyāpyatā: pervadedness, the property of being pervaded
vyāpyatva: pervadedness, the property of being pervaded
vyāpakatā: pervaderness, the property of being the pervader
vyāpakatva: pervaderness, the property of being the pervader

parāmarśa.n: The cognition that the subject possesses a probans pervaded by the probandum (‘this hill has smoke pervaded by fire’); for Nyāya it is what directly produces the inference.

liṅgaparāmarśa: consideration of the mark: cognising the probans as pervaded and as present in the subject
anumiti: inferential cognition, the conclusion an inference produces
upamiti: cognition from comparison: learning that a word names a certain kind of thing
pakṣatā: subjecthood — the condition of the subject that allows inference (the absence of certainty about the probandum unaccompanied by a desire to infer)
pakṣadharmatā: presence of the probans in the subject
sapakṣa: similar instance — a place where the probandum is known to be present (e.g. the kitchen)
vipakṣa: dissimilar instance — a place where the probandum is known to be absent (e.g. a lake)
liṅgin: the bearer of the mark; what is inferred

upādhi.n: A property that pervades the probandum but not the probans; its presence shows the concomitance is only conditional (e.g. contact with wet fuel when inferring smoke from fire).

sopādhika: conditional, vitiated by an adjunct (of a concomitance)
anvaya: positive concomitance (‘where X, there Y’); also the syntactic connection of words
vyatireka: negative concomitance (‘where no Y, there no X’); difference, exclusion
anvayavyatirekin: a probans with both positive and negative concomitance
kevalānvayin: purely positive (probans or property) — one with no negative instance, e.g. knowability
kevalavyatirekin: purely negative probans — with no positive example apart from the subject itself
sādhāraṇa: common; (as a pseudo-reason) inconclusive because present where the probandum is absent
asādhāraṇa: uncommon, specific; (as a pseudo-reason) inconclusive because found only in the subject; (of a cause) special
anupasaṃhārin: non-conclusive pseudo-reason — one with no example at all, because everything is the subject
satpratipakṣa: counterbalanced (pseudo-reason) — met by an equally strong reason for the opposite
āśrayāsiddha: unestablished as to its locus — the subject does not exist (e.g. a sky-lotus)
svarūpāsiddha: unestablished in itself — the probans is not present in the subject
vyāpyatvāsiddha: unestablished as pervaded — the concomitance is vitiated by an adjunct
bādhita: contradicted (pseudo-reason) — the absence of the probandum is known by another means of knowledge
bādha: contradiction, sublation by a stronger cognition

avacchedaka.n: The property under which something is taken: e.g. smokeness is the delimitor of the probans-hood that resides in smoke. Central to Navya-Nyāya precision.

avacchedakatā: delimitorness, the property of being the delimitor
avacchedakatva: delimitorness, the property of being the delimitor
avacchinna: delimited (by), specified as (e.g. ‘ghaṭatvāvacchinna’ = taken as a pot)

pratiyogin.n: The thing whose absence, or whose relation, is in question: a pot is the counterpositive of ‘the absence of a pot’.

pratiyogitā: counterpositiveness, the property of being the counterpositive
pratiyogitva: counterpositiveness, the property of being the counterpositive
anuyogin: subjunct, locus — the thing in which a relation or absence resides (the floor in ‘absence of a pot on the floor’)
anuyogitā: subjunctness, the property of being the locus of a relation
nirūpaka: describer — the correlate that determines a relational property
nirūpita: described by, correlated with (a relational property determined by its correlate)
prakāra: qualifier, mode — the feature under which a thing is cognised
prakāratā: qualifierness — the content-feature of a cognition corresponding to its qualifier
prakāraka: having as its qualifier (‘tat-prakāraka’ = in which that is the qualifier)
saprakāraka: having a qualifier, determinate (of a cognition)
viśeṣya: qualificand — the thing qualified in a cognition
viśeṣyatā: qualificandness — the property of being the qualificand in a cognition
viśeṣaṇatā: qualifierness; the ‘attributive’ (self-linking) relation, e.g. of an absence to its locus
viśeṣaṇatva: the property of being a qualifier
viṣayatā: objecthood, content — the property of being an object of a cognition
viṣayitā: the property a cognition has of being about an object
saṃsarga: relation, connection (especially the relational element in a cognition)
saṃsargatā: the property of being the relation (in a cognition)
svarūpasambandha: self-linking relation — a relation that is nothing but the nature of its terms
tādātmya: identity (the relation whose denial is mutual absence)
vṛtti: occurrence, residence in a locus; also, the signifying function of a word
vṛttitā: occurrence, the property of residing in something
vṛttitva: occurrence, the property of residing in something
adhikaraṇatā: locushood, the property of being the locus
ādheya: the located, what resides in a locus
ādheyatā: locatedness, the property of residing in a locus
samānādhikaraṇa: co-located, occurring in the same locus
sāmānādhikaraṇya: co-location, occurrence in the same locus
vyadhikaraṇa: located elsewhere, occurring in a different locus
avyāpti: under-coverage — a definition failing to cover some of what it should
ativyāpti: over-coverage — a definition extending to what it should not
asambhava: impossibility — a definition that fits nothing at all
lakṣaṇā: secondary signification, indication (a word conveying something related to its primary meaning)
śakti: denotative power, the primary meaning-relation of a word
śakya: primary meaning, what a word denotes
śaktigraha: grasping the denotative power, learning what a word means
ākāṅkṣā: syntactic expectancy (between the words of a sentence)
yogyatā: semantic compatibility, fitness (of the meanings to be connected)
tātparya: intention, purport (of a speaker or sentence)
śābdabodha: verbal cognition, the understanding produced by a sentence
nirvikalpaka: non-conceptual (cognition), apprehending a thing without a qualifier
savikalpaka: conceptual (cognition), apprehending a thing as qualified (‘this is a pot’)
samavāyin: inherent; the substrate in which something inheres
samavāyikāraṇa: inherent (material) cause — the substrate in which the effect inheres, e.g. threads for cloth
asamavāyikāraṇa: non-inherent cause — a cause inhering in the same thing as the effect or its cause, e.g. the conjunction of threads
nimittakāraṇa: instrumental (efficient) cause — neither inherent nor non-inherent, e.g. loom and shuttle
karaṇa: instrument — the special (asādhāraṇa) cause of a result
kāraṇatā: causehood, the property of being a cause
kāraṇatva: causehood, the property of being a cause
kāryatā: effecthood, the property of being an effect
anyathāsiddha: ‘otherwise established’ — a mere accompaniment, not a genuine cause
anyathāsiddhi: being ‘otherwise established’, i.e. not a genuine cause
prāgabhāva: prior absence — the non-existence of an effect before it arises (beginningless, but it ends)
pradhvaṃsa: destruction, posterior absence (it begins, but has no end)
atyantābhāva: absolute absence — absence of a thing in a locus at all times
anyonyābhāva: mutual absence, difference (‘a pot is not a cloth’)
dvyaṇuka: dyad, the compound of two atoms
tryaṇuka: triad, the smallest perceptible substance (three dyads)
saṃskāra: impression, disposition — one of the qualities: velocity, memory-impression, elasticity
bhāvanā: memory-impression, the disposition that causes recollection
sthitisthāpaka: elasticity — the disposition that restores a thing to its former state
paratva: remoteness in space, or seniority in time (a quality)
aparatva: nearness in space, or juniority in time (a quality)
sneha: viscidity — the quality of water that makes powder cohere
pākaja: produced by heating (of qualities that change when a thing is baked)
sāṃsiddhika: natural, innate (e.g. the fluidity of water)
naimittika: occasioned, due to a cause (e.g. the fluidity of melted ghee)
anubhava: experience, presentative cognition (as opposed to memory)
viparyaya: error, misapprehension (e.g. taking mother-of-pearl for silver)
dharmin: property-bearer, the substratum of a property
pratibandhaka: obstructor, a factor that prevents an effect
āpādaka: (in reductio) what would entail the consequence
anuvyavasāya: apperception — the after-cognition by which a cognition is itself known (‘I know the pot’)
jñānalakṣaṇā: extraordinary contact through a cognition (by which a remembered feature is perceived)
sāmānyalakṣaṇā: extraordinary contact through a universal, by which all its instances are presented
arthāpatti: presumption, postulation (to explain what is otherwise inexplicable)
anupalabdhi: non-apprehension (claimed by Mīmāṃsā as the means of knowing absence)
svatastva: intrinsicness (of validity), being known or produced by the cognition’s own conditions
paratastva: extrinsicness (of validity), depending on further conditions

apūrva.m: ‘the new’ — the unseen potency a ritual act produces, which yields its fruit later
apūrva.n: A Mīmāṃsā notion that Gaṅgeśa examines in the Apūrvavāda.

vidhi: injunction; the meaning of the optative and imperative suffixes
iṣṭasādhanatā: being a means to what is desired
iṣṭasādhanatva: being a means to what is desired
maṅgala: auspicious invocation (at the beginning of a work)
śiṣṭācāra: the practice of the cultured (as evidence for an injunction)
gaurava: prolixity, theoretical heaviness (a reason to reject a view)
vinigamanāviraha: absence of a deciding reason between alternatives
siddhasādhana: proving what is already established (a fault)
iṣṭāpatti: acceptance of the consequence (‘we welcome that’)
pūrvapakṣa: the prima facie view, the opponent’s position
prābhākara: follower of Prabhākara’s school of Mīmāṃsā
bhāṭṭa: follower of Kumārila Bhaṭṭa’s school of Mīmāṃsā
mūla: root text (here the Tarkasaṃgraha itself); root, basis
dīpikā: ‘lamp’; the Dīpikā, Annaṃbhaṭṭa’s commentary on his Tarkasaṃgraha
prakāśikā: the Prakāśikā, Nīlakaṇṭha’s sub-commentary on the Dīpikā
anugama: a single formulation that covers all the cases
ananugama: lack of a single formulation covering all cases
ghaṭa: pot, jar (the standard example of an object)
mahānasa: kitchen — the standard example of a place with smoke and fire
mahāhrada: great lake — the standard example of a place without fire or smoke
parvata: hill, mountain — the standard subject of inference
gavaya: gavaya, a wild ox (the standard example in comparison)
śukti: mother-of-pearl (mistaken for silver in the standard example of error)
sthāṇu: post, stump (doubted to be a man in the standard example of doubt)
abhidheya: nameable, what can be denoted by a word
ayutasiddha: inseparably related (two things of which one exists only as resting on the other)
